newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers end arguments, Megan's Law case goes to jury.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers end arguments, Megan's Law case goes to jury.

text.p: Final arguments ended on Wednesday in the Megan Kanka murder trial with the prosecution describing the defendant as a calculating killer and the defence saying he took the blame for an accidential slaying.

Jesse Timmendequas, charged in the July 29, 1994, murder that inspired Megan's Law, sat expressionless as prosecutor Kathryn Flicker described in ghastly detail how he lured the 7-year-old girl into his home, raped and strangled her and later dumped her body "like so much garbage" in a local park.
"He committed unmitigated evil...," Flicker said. "He could have stopped, but he didn't. His acts were so perverse that they shock our collective conscience."

The prosecution's two-hour summation became so emotional that the defence sought a mistrial, saying the language was so emotive it would colour the jury's deliberations. Mercer County Superior Court Judge Andrew Smithson denied the request, but told the jury to disregard the prosecution's hyperbole.

The girl's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, listened silently during the summations. Mrs. Kanka sometimes buried her head in her hands. She dabbed at tears when she heard her daughter's body was covered with insects when police found it in weeds and tall grass.
Timmendequas' defence attorney, Barbara Lependorf, in a three-hour summation said the defendant was a victim and suggested he was protecting one or both of his roommates.
Timmendequas, 36, lived with two other men across the street from the Kanka family. He confessed to the crimes and led police to the body.

Lependorf argued that the roommates' alibis were not watertight and that Timmendequas' confessions were not reliable because he gave six somewhat different versions of the crime. She added that he is of low intelligence and easily influenced.

"I suggest to you that Jesse is a victim," Lependorf told jurors. "He obviously had guilty knowledge. I wouldn't insult you by saying otherwise. He knew what went on in that house. He was involved. But how much? To what extent?"
The jury is expected to begin deliberations on Thursday.
The crime sparked a public outcry because the girl's parents had not known that Timmendequas was a sex offender twice convicted in assaults involving girls aged 7 and 5.

Megan's Law was the result of the family's impassioned campaigning. Originally the law required sex offenders to register with authorities and empowered authorities to notify the public about those they regarded as posing the highest risk.

But a series of rulings left the state with the power to require registration but not to notify the public and that aspect of the law is being challenged in federal court. Critics say Megan's Law violates the Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served out their sentences.
Most other states have similar laws and in 1996 President Clinton signed a law making it easier for residents to get information about released sex offenders.
